title: Multicenter characterization of enterocolitis associated with BCMA-directed CAR T cell therapy - Nature Medicine
byline: Mikkilineni; Lekha; Hamilton; Mark P; Jensen; Alexandria; Lim; Kenneth JC; Galarza-Fortuna; Gliceida M; Kumar; Anupama D; Ferreri; Christopher J; Portuguese; An
html:
Abstract

Immune effector cell-associated enterocolitis (IEC-EC) is a delayed toxicity of ciltacabtagene autoleucel. The US Multiple Myeloma Immunotherapy Consortium retrospectively adjudicated 54 suspected cases from 8 institutions: 41 were IEC-EC (31 confirmed by anti-camelid variable heavy-chain immunohistochemistry, 10 probable). Through September 2025, cumulative incidence was 3.0% (39 of 1,308 ciltacabtagene autoleucel recipients; 95% CI 2.1–4.1%); 12-month competing-risk incidence was 3.0% (95% CI 2.1–4.1%). Median symptom onset was 75 days after infusion. Grade ≥3 diarrhea occurred in 85% (34 of 40 with diarrhea); 73% (30 of 41) required parenteral nutrition. Despite normal upper endoscopy in 41% (9 of 22), duodenal biopsies showed villous blunting, apoptotic bodies and a dense cytotoxic T cell infiltrate, CD4+ in 61% (19 of 31), CD8+ in 26% (8 of 31) and mixed in 13% (4 of 31). A dominant T cell clone was detected in 76% (13 of 17 tested). Delayed neurotoxicity co-occurred in 41% (17 of 41). At last follow-up, 32% (13 of 41) resolved, 27% (11 of 41) had ongoing symptoms and 41% (17 of 41) died with active IEC-EC. Combined biologic and T cell-directed therapy yielded the highest resolution (55%, 6 of 11) in small subgroups. IEC-EC is potentially fatal and requires systematic evaluation and early directed therapy.

Main

Immune effector cell-associated enterocolitis (IEC-EC) has emerged as a rare1 but serious delayed toxicity following B cell maturation antigen (BCMA)-directed chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) T cell therapy for multiple myeloma (MM), particularly ciltacabtagene autoleucel (cilta-cel)2,3. Early published cases describe severe presentations with substantial morbidity and mortality with an overall incidence of 1.2% (ref. 1) following BCMA-targeting CAR T cell therapy and 2.2% (ref. 1) following cilta-cel therapy1,4,5,6,7,8. However, these reports relied on locally reviewed pathology and lacked standardized diagnostic criteria. The importance of this toxicity was underscored by the United States (US) Food and Drug Administration revision of the cilta-cel prescribing information in 20259,10, with a boxed warning citing severe diarrhea, weight loss and fatal outcomes. Without standardized diagnostic criteria, there is risk of both under-recognizing IEC-EC and over-attributing nonspecific gastrointestinal (GI) symptoms to this entity. To address these gaps, the US Multiple Myeloma Immunotherapy Consortium, a multi-institutional academic collaborative, convened the multidisciplinary IEC-EC Working Group, which aggregated suspected post-cilta-cel GI toxicity cases from eight academic institutions with the goals of (1) defining the clinicopathologic spectrum of IEC-EC, (2) estimating the cumulative incidence of IEC-EC, (3) establishing a diagnostic framework for practitioners to improve early identification and workup of these patients, (4) describing treatment approaches and their observed outcomes, and (5) identifying future research directions (Fig. 1a).

a, Study design and case-ascertainment workflow. The IEC-EC Working Group of the US Multiple Myeloma Immunotherapy Consortium established five aims and a structured workflow for case identification, data collection, central pathology review and multidisciplinary tumor board adjudication. Cases were submitted from eight US academic institutions. Central histopathologic review by consortium pathologists included anti-camelid VHH IHC and T cell clonality assessment when feasible. b, Flow diagram of case classification. Of 54 suspected cases reviewed, one (patient 25, a 2019 clinical-trial case outside the study window and incompletely characterized) was non-evaluable and excluded from the cohort and all denominators. Of the 53 classified cases, 41 (77%) met criteria for IEC-EC (31 confirmed by anti-camelid VHH IHC; 10 probable, of whom 4 had central pathology review and 6 were classified on clinical history alone) and 12 (23%) were negative. Among the 41 IEC-EC cases, 17 (41%) died with active IEC-EC, 11 (27%) had ongoing symptoms and 13 (32%) achieved resolution at last follow-up. Of the 17 deaths, 10 were due to infectious complications during active disease (infection was the primary cause in 8), 5 were directly attributable to IEC-EC or its complications and 2 were from other causes (embolic cerebrovascular accident, n = 1; Parkinsonism, n = 1). One additional patient (patient 41) died of progressive myeloma after IEC-EC had resolved and is counted among the 13 resolved cases; all-cause mortality was 18 of 41 (44%). Previously published cases are identified in Methods.

Results

Of 54 suspected cases reviewed, each was discussed at the working group multidisciplinary tumor board and underwent central pathology evaluation when diagnostic tissue was available. Diagnostic confirmation was based on anti-camelid variable heavy-chain (VHH) domain immunohistochemistry (IHC), an assay targeting the camelid-derived binding domain of the cilta-cel CAR construct that identifies CAR+ T cells in tissue sections. Cases were classified as confirmed IEC-EC (≥20% VHH-positive lamina propria lymphocytes), probable IEC-EC (consistent clinical and/or histopathologic features without VHH IHC confirmation) or negative (<5% VHH-positive cells or self-limited symptoms without pathologic evaluation) (Fig. 1b and Table 1; full criteria are found in Methods; severity and outcome definitions are given in Supplementary Tables 1 and 2). No case had a diagnostic biopsy in the indeterminate 5% to 20% VHH IHC range, although levels of camelid VHH between 5% and 20% were seen in biopsies after immunosuppressive therapy initiation and during the treatment course. Anti-camelid VHH IHC was available at five institutions during the study period (Stanford University, MD Anderson Cancer Center, Mayo Clinic, Moffitt Cancer Center and Lombardi Comprehensive Cancer Center). Probable cases most commonly lacked VHH IHC confirmation owing to assay unavailability at the treating institution or lack of diagnostic tissue.

Patient characteristics

The 54 suspected cases of post-cilta-cel GI toxicity were identified across 8 academic institutions between 2019 and 2025. Although the call for cases was inclusive of all BCMA-directed CAR T cell products, only cases following cilta-cel were submitted, potentially reflecting current clinical-use patterns. One patient (patient 25), treated on the CARTITUDE-1 trial (NCT03548207) in 2019, developed diarrhea on day 778, clinically consistent with IEC-EC, with a diagnostic biopsy on day 1,317. The tumor board adjudicated this case non-evaluable and excluded it from the IEC-EC cohort and all denominators for two reasons: it reflected single-site 2019 clinical-trial treatment outside the 2022 to September 2025 real-world window, and its only anti-camelid VHH-stained biopsy (day 1,317) was negative, obtained without confirmed systematic random duodenal and ileal sampling, and was discordant with autopsy-confirmed colitis (tissue not available for camelid-VHH IHC), leaving the case neither confirmed nor confidently negative. The following characteristics describe the 53 evaluable patients.

Across all 53 patients, the median follow-up from cilta-cel infusion was 397 days (interquartile range (IQR), 210–822 days). The median age was 67 years (IQR, 62, 72), with male patients representing 70% of the population. Demographics by diagnostic category are presented in Table 2. Patients received a median of 4 (IQR, 3, 5) previous lines of therapy. High-risk cytogenetics (defined as presence of del(17p), t(4;14) or t(14;16)) were present in 36% of patients and extramedullary disease was present in 15%.

Bridging therapy preceded infusion in 38 of 41 patients with IEC-EC (93%); among 32 evaluable patients, 6 (19%) achieved a partial response or better (Supplementary Figs. 1–3). CAR T cell course and treatment data are summarized in Table 3.

Of the 53 evaluable cases, 12 (23%) were negative for IEC-EC. Ten had GI symptoms prompting endoscopic evaluation, with anti-camelid VHH IHC showing fewer than 5% positive lymphocytes in the lamina propria in all 10 cases. Alternative etiologies were identified in four of these patients, including infectious gastroenteritis (n = 2), bile acid malabsorption (n = 1) and medication toxicity (n = 1); the remaining six patients had self-limited symptoms that resolved without immunosuppressive therapy. Two additional cases without endoscopic evaluation had mild, self-limited symptoms that resolved without intervention. Notably, one patient (patient 52) with fewer than 5% VHH-positive cells carried a separate diagnosis of a CAR+ peripheral T cell lymphoma (PTCL).

Incidence estimation

Extended Data Table 1 details the cumulative incidence calculations. The raw incidence and competing-risk estimates agreed, suggesting that competing mortality had minimal impact on the estimate. Overall cumulative incidence was estimated as follows: (1) raw estimation: 3.0% (95% CI 2.1–4.1%); (2) 12-month competing risk model: 3.0% (95% CI 2.1–4.1%); and (3) sensitivity 12-month competing risk model: 3.0% (95% CI 2.1–4.2%). These estimates derive from a retrospective, referral-based case series assembled across the participating consortium institutions and should be interpreted as consortium-based rather than a definitive population-level incidence. Cumulative incidence showed an overall increase with year-to-year variation, from approximately 2.1% in 2022 to 3.6% from January to September 2025, using the 12-month cumulative incidence estimates. Among the 39 IEC-EC cases through September 2025, 15 (38.5%) were female, 7 (17.9%) identified as Black and 11 (28.2%) as non-White, compared with 43.2%, 10.2% and 20.1%, respectively, among the overall population of 1,308 cilta-cel-treated patients. The raw cumulative incidence of IEC-EC was numerically higher among Black (5.3%) and non-White (4.2%) patients than in the overall population (3.0%). However, chi-square tests of proportions did not find an overrepresentation of female (two sided; χ2 = 0.18; DoF = 1; P = 0.671), Black (two sided; χ2 = 1.70; DoF = 1; P = 0.193) or non-White (two sided; χ2 = 1.07; DoF = 1; P = 0.300) patients with IEC-EC compared with the overall cilta-cel population. No tested variable (peak absolute lymphocyte count (ALC), ferritin and C-reactive protein (CRP), extramedullary disease, high-risk cytogenetics, high marrow plasma-cell burden) differed significantly between IEC-EC and negative cases (Extended Data Table 2).

IEC-EC cohort

Of the 53 evaluable cases, 41 (77%) were adjudicated as IEC-EC. Within the IEC-EC cohort (n = 41), 31 were confirmed by VHH IHC (76%) and 10 were probable (24%), defined as cases with clinical and/or histopathologic features consistent with IEC-EC but without anti-camelid VHH IHC confirmation. Full definitions are included in Methods. Of the ten probable cases, four had pathology available for central review, showing a CD3+ T cell infiltrate on GI tissue biopsy without VHH-confirmation testing. The remaining six probable cases were classified on clinical history alone in the absence of tissue for central pathology review.

The median time from cilta-cel infusion to GI symptom onset in the IEC-EC cohort (n = 41) was 75 days (range 14–541). Diarrhea was the dominant symptom; of the 40 patients with diarrhea, 34 (85%) had a Common Terminology Criteria for Adverse Events grade ≥3 and 2 had low grades (grade 1 or 2); grades were not recorded in 4 patients. One patient presented with abdominal pain without diarrhea.

Laboratory parameters of the 41 patients with IEC-EC after CAR T cell infusion (day 0 to day 30) were as follows: median baseline ferritin was 221.5 ng ml−1 (IQR 82.8–400.3), rising to a peak of 578 ng ml−1 (IQR 299.5–1,318.8) at a median of day 9; median baseline CRP was 2.2 mg dl−1 (IQR 0.6–3.8), rising to 28.4 mg dl−1 (IQR 5.8–56.1) at a median of day 8; and peak ALC was 4.8 × 109 l−1 (IQR 1.9–11.2) at a median of day 13.

Total parenteral nutrition (TPN) was required in 30 patients (73%). At last follow-up, 13 patients (32%) had achieved IEC-EC resolution, 11 (27%) had ongoing symptoms and 17 (41%) had died in the setting of active IEC-EC. Of these 17 deaths, 10 resulted from infectious complications (predominantly septic shock and gram-negative bacteremia; infection was the primary cause in 8), 5 were directly attributable to IEC-EC complications (profound diarrhea, ileus, perforation) and 2 from other causes (embolic cerebrovascular accident and Parkinsonism). One additional patient (patient 41), whose IEC-EC had resolved, subsequently died of unrelated progressive myeloma and was classified as resolved rather than as an IEC-EC-attributable death; all-cause cohort mortality was 18 of 41 (44%). Individual clinical courses are shown in Fig. 2a and characteristics by outcome in Extended Data Table 3. Overall survival for the cohort was 66.7% (95% CI 48.6–79.6%) at 12 months and 52.2% (95% CI 31.9–69.1%) at 24 months (Fig. 2b)
